correctness.rationale: For one index and two susceptible contacts, conditioning on the Gamma infectious period gives P0=L(2lambda) and P1=2L(lambda)[L(lambda)-L(2lambda)], including secondary transmission. The positive quadratic root recovers p=L(lambda), and Gamma Laplace ratios give log(q)/log(p)=log(1+2u)/log(1+u). Strict convexity of (1+u)log(1+u) proves this scalar map is decreasing from 2 to 1 and hence globally invertible. Subsequently a, lambda, beta and eta are explicitly recovered, including eta endpoints. A nonzero 2x2 minor of the two-means map and the implicit-function theorem establish a one-dimensional family of indistinguishable interior triples. The variance expansion gives q-p^2=lambda^2/a+O(lambda^3). Standalone rational enumeration of all 64 possible three-person directed arc graphs for four Gamma shapes and multiple inversion checks reproduced the formulas. No infinite-parameter proof relies on that finite check.

value.rationale: The smallest nontrivial pair of household sizes supplies a naturally motivated data-reporting problem from the source: can varying infectious-period shape, contact rate and household-size exponent all be disentangled? The theorem gives a globally unique inverse from three exact observables, an explicit reason why only two average secondary attack fractions are insufficient, and the sharp low-transmission weakness of the shape signal. It informs whether outbreak datasets must retain final-size frequencies rather than just attack rates; the result is not merely a table entry or trivial numeric instance. Its scope is limited to single-introduction, homogeneous Gamma-duration SIR households of sizes two and three and exact population laws.
